      "text": "\n\n\nThis is a fantastic question and gets right to the heart of the difference between pure math and applied physics. \n\nTo answer your question simply: **No, the general formula is not enough for practical applications because it contains an unknown constant ($C$) that prevents you from calculating an actual, real-world number.**\n\nHere is a breakdown of why we need both steps:\n\n### 1. The General Solution gives you the \"Pattern\" (Shape)\nLook at the result of part **a)** in your image: \n$m(t) \u003d Ce^{-\\beta t}$\n\nThrough integration, we found the *shape* of how the substance behaves. We know it decays exponentially. However, because of the rules of calculus, integration always leaves us with an arbitrary constant, **$C$**. \n\nIf you are a scientist in a lab and you want to know how much mass ($m$) is left after 5 seconds ($t\u003d5$), you **cannot** solve this equation. You can plug in $t\u003d5$, and you might know the decay rate $\\beta$, but you are stuck because you don\u0027t know what $C$ is. \n\nThe general solution represents an *infinite family* of possible decay curves. It tells you *how* it decays, but not *where it started*.\n\n### 2. The Particular Solution gives you the \"Reality\" (Actual values)\nTo make the equation useful in the real world, we have to find out what $C$ is. We do this using an **Initial Condition** (začetni pogoj), which is what part **b)** is doing.\n\nIn the real world, you always know how much material you *started* with. Let\u0027s say you put 100 grams of a radioactive isotope on a scale right now. \n* \"Right now\" means time zero: $t \u003d 0$.\n* The mass right now is $m_0$: $m(0) \u003d 100$.\n\nWhen you plug $t\u003d0$ into the general equation, $e^{-\\beta \\cdot 0}$ becomes $e^0$, which is just $1$. Therefore, you find out that $C$ is exactly equal to your starting mass ($m_0$). \n\nNow your equation becomes the **Particular Solution**:\n$m(t) \u003d m_0e^{-\\beta t}$\n\n**Why is this better?** Because now there are no unknown mathematical constants. Every letter in this equation is a real-world parameter you can measure or plug in:\n* $m_0$ \u003d Starting mass (e.g., 100g)\n* $\\beta$ \u003d Decay coefficient (known for specific materials)\n* $t$ \u003d Time elapsed\n\n*Now* you can fill in the parameters and actually calculate exactly how much mass is left tomorrow. \n\n***\n\n### A Non-Math Analogy: Driving a Car\nImagine the differential equation is the speedometer of your car. \n* **Differential Equation:** \"You are driving at a constant speed of 100 km/h.\"\n* **General Solution:** \"Your location is $100 \\cdot (\\text{hours}) + C$.\" \n\nIf I ask you, \"Where are you after 2 hours?\" you can\u0027t tell me. You know you drove 200 km, but you don\u0027t know your final location because you don\u0027t know your starting point ($C$).\n\n* **Particular Solution (Initial Condition):** \"At hour 0, I started in Ljubljana ($C \u003d \\text{Ljubljana}$).\"\nNow, the formula is: Location \u003d $100 \\cdot (\\text{hours}) + \\text{Ljubljana}$. \n*Now* you know that after 2 hours, you are 200 km away from Ljubljana. \n\n**Summary:** The differential equation gives you the rule. The general solution gives you the pattern. The particular solution anchors that pattern to reality so you can do actual math with it.",

      "text": "\n\n\nYou have hit upon one of the most notoriously confusing naming conventions in all of calculus! Your professor is absolutely right, and your confusion is completely justified. \n\nMathematicians reused the exact same word—**\"homogeneous\"**—to describe two **completely different concepts** in differential equations. \n\nHere is the breakdown of why *this* equation is called homogeneous, and how it differs from the \"homogeneous part\" you will learn about later.\n\n---\n\n### 1. First-Order \"Homogeneous\" Equations (The Image)\nIn the context of the page you uploaded, the word \"homogeneous\" refers to the **algebraic properties of the terms**. \n\nIn algebra, a function is \"homogeneous of degree zero\" if you can multiply both $x$ and $y$ by some constant $t$, and the $t$\u0027s completely cancel out. Mathematically: $f(tx, ty) \u003d f(x, y)$.\n\nLet\u0027s look at the specific example (Zgled 2.3) from your image: \n$y\u0027 \u003d \\frac{x + y}{x - y}$\n\nIf you replace every $x$ with $tx$ and every $y$ with $ty$, look what happens:\n$$y\u0027 \u003d \\frac{tx + ty}{tx - ty} \u003d \\frac{t(x + y)}{t(x - y)}$$\n\nBecause there is a $t$ in every single term, you can factor it out of the top and bottom, and they cancel each other out completely, leaving you right back where you started: $\\frac{x+y}{x-y}$.\n\n**Why does this matter?**\nBecause if an equation has this special algebraic property, it guarantees that you can divide the top and bottom by $x$ to force every variable to look exactly like the fraction **$\\frac{y}{x}$**. \n$$\\frac{\\frac{x}{x} + \\frac{y}{x}}{\\frac{x}{x} - \\frac{y}{x}} \u003d \\frac{1 + \\frac{y}{x}}{1 - \\frac{y}{x}}$$\n\nBecause the whole right side of the equation can be written strictly as a function of $(\\frac{y}{x})$, you can use the \"Homogeneous Substitution method\" shown in your notes: introducing a new variable **$u \u003d \\frac{y}{x}$**. \n\n### 2. Linear \"Homogeneous\" Equations (The Later Methods)\nLater in your course, you will solve higher-order linear differential equations that look something like this:\n$y\u0027\u0027 + 3y\u0027 + 2y \u003d 10 \\sin(x)$\n\nHere, the word \"homogeneous\" means something totally different. In this context, **homogeneous simply means \"equals zero.\"** \n\nIf an equation has no standalone $x$-terms (meaning every term contains either $y$ or a derivative of $y$), it equals 0 and is called homogeneous:\n$y\u0027\u0027 + 3y\u0027 + 2y \u003d 0$ *(This is a homogeneous linear DE)*\n\nWhen you have a non-homogeneous equation (like the one equaling $10 \\sin(x)$), the method to solve it involves first pretending it equals zero. You solve that \"homogeneous part\" to find the general shape (the complementary solution, $y_c$), and then you use other methods to find the specific solution for the $10 \\sin(x)$ part (the particular solution, $y_p$).\n\n---\n\n### Summary\n*   **Context 1 (Your image):** \"Homogeneous\" means the terms share the same algebraic degree, allowing the $t$\u0027s to cancel out. This lets you turn all the variables into **$\\frac{y}{x}$** and use the $u \u003d \\frac{y}{x}$ substitution.\n*   **Context 2 (Your lectures):** \"Homogeneous\" means the right-hand side of a linear differential equation **equals $0$** (there is no external \"forcing\" function).\n\nYou just have to memorize that the math community uses one word for two completely unrelated tricks!",

        "text": "ogeneous\" Equations (The Later Methods)\nLater in your course, you will solve higher-order linear differential equations that"

      }, {
        "text": "\n\nHere, the word \"homogeneous\" means something totally different. In this context, **homogeneous simply means \"equals zero"

      }, {

      }, {
        "text": " \"homogeneous part\" to find the general shape (the complementary solution, $y_c$), and then you use other"
      }, {
        "text": " methods to find the specific solution for the $10 \\sin(x)$ part (the particular solution, $y"
      }, {
        "text": "_p$).\n\n---\n\n### Summary\n*   **Context 1 (Your image):** \"Homogeneous\" means"
      }, {

      }, {

      }, {
        "text": "\n*   **Context 2 (Your lectures):** \"Homogeneous\" means the right-hand side of a linear differential equation **"
      }, {

The \"Homogeneous\" part (Pretending it equals 0)**\n$y\u0027\u0027 + 3y\u0027 + 2y \u003d 0$\nPretending the equation equals 0 is the mathematical equivalent of asking: *\"How does the car\u0027s suspension behave if the road is perfectly flat?\"* \nIf you push the hood of the car down and let go, it will naturally bounce up and down a few times and then settle. Because of a mathematical rule called **Linearity** (Superposition). \nThe total bouncing of the car is:\n`[Natural bouncing of the springs (equals 0)] +[Bouncing caused by the road (equals 10sin(x))]`\n\nIf you plug both parts into the left side of the equation together:\n$0 + 10 \\sin(x) \u003d 10 \\sin(x)$\n\nIf you *didn\u0027t* pretend it equals 0 first, you would only find the bouncing caused by the road. You would completely miss the natural bouncing of the car itself! We need the \"equals 0\" part because that\u0027s where the $+C_1$ and $+C_2$ live, which allows us to adapt the formula to any starting condition (like whether the car started at the bottom of a pothole or the top of a hill).\n\n---\n\n### Part 2: Why are DEs solved in such an annoying, non-obvious way?\n\nYou mentioned hating that there is no obvious way to solve them. I am giving you a pile of dust and broken glass (the derivative) and saying: **\"Reverse engineer the exact vase this used to be.\"**\n\nThere is no \"forward\" algorithm for reverse engineering. You can\u0027t just put the dust into a machine and press \"solve.\" Instead, mathematicians over the last 300 years had to look at the pile of glass and say:\n*   *\"Hmm, this glass is green. I know that vases shaped like $e^x$ are green. Let\u0027s pretend the answer is $e^x$, plug it in, and see if it works.\"*\n\nThis method of \"educated guessing\" is formally called an **Ansatz** (German for \"approach\" or \"initial placement\"). \nWhen you learn DEs, you aren\u0027t actually learning how to \"solve\" them step-by-step.       }, {
        "text": " the case where $g(x) \u003d 0$. We get the homogeneous part).\n\nThe left side of the"
      }, {
        "text": " equation ($y\u0027 + f(x)y$) defines the **\"rules of the system\"** itself."
      }, {
        "text": " \n* If this were a bank account, $f(x)$ represents the bank\u0027s interest rate. \n*"
      }, {
        "text": " If this were a cup of coffee, $f(x)$ represents how poorly the mug holds in heat.\n\nSolving"
      }, {
        "text": " the equation for $0$ gives you $y_h$ (the homogeneous solution). This is the **natural,"
      }, {
        "text": " baseline behavior** of the system if no one is interfering with it. It is entirely independent of $g(x)$."
      }, {
        "text": " And crucially, $y_h$ is where your constant $+C$ lives, meaning it handles the \"initial conditions\" (like"
      }, {
        "text": " how hot the coffee was when you poured it).\n\n### 2. \"Finding a representative $y_p$ that"
      }, {
        "text": " gives the whole $y$ the direction of $g(x)$\"\nYour use of the word \"representative\""
      }, {
        "text": " is incredibly mathematically accurate. \n\nWe call it the **particular** solution ($y_p$) because we literally just need to find"
      }, {
        "text": " **one single, specific mathematical function** that satisfies the $g(x)$ part. We don\u0027t need a $+"
      }, {
        "text": "C$ for this part. We don\u0027t need a general formula. We just need *one representative example* of"
      }, {
        "text": " how the system responds to the external force $g(x)$.\n\n* Back to the bank account: $g("
      }, {
        "text": "x)$ is you depositing a specific amount of money every month. \n* $y_p$ is the exact mathematical \""
      }, {
        "text": "direction\" or \"trend\" your money takes because of those deposits.\n\n### Why adding them together ($y \u003d y_"
      }, {
        "text": "h + y_p$) works beautifully:\nBecause the equation is **Linear**, the math lets you literally just add the \""
      }, {
        "text": "unforced\" baseline behavior ($y_h$) together with the \"forced\" representative behavior ($y_p$) to get the total"
      }, {
        "text": ", perfect reality ($y$).\n\nHere is the simple, beautiful proof of what you just realized:\n* We know that the"
      }, {
        "text": " baseline system equals zero: **$y_h\u0027 + f(x)y_h \u003d 0$**"
      }, {
        "text": "\n* We know our representative forced system equals $g(x)$: **$y_p\u0027 + f(x"
      }, {
        "text": ")y_p \u003d g(x)$**\n\nIf you define your final answer as $y \u003d y_h"
      }, {
        "text": " + y_p$, plug it into the left side of your textbook\u0027s equation:\n$$(y_h +"
      }, {
        "text": " y_p)\u0027 + f(x)(y_h + y_p)$$\n\nExpand it out:\n$$y_"
      }, {
        "text": "h\u0027 + y_p\u0027 + f(x)y_h + f(x)y_p$$"
      }, {
        "text": "\n\nGroup the $y_h$ parts and the $y_p$ parts together:\n$$"
      }, {
        "text": "[ y_h\u0027 + f(x)y_h ] + [ y_p\u0027 + f(x)y_p ]$$"
      }, {
        "text": "\n\nLook at what happens based on what we know:\n$$[ 0 ] + [ g(x) ] \u003d g("
      }, {
        "text": "x)$$\n\n**You solved it!** \nBy pretending the equation equals 0 to get the $C$"
      }, {
        "text": " (the $y_h$), and then finding one single representative function that perfectly matches the \"driver\" $g(x)$"
      }, {
        "text": " (the $y_p$), you completely map out the real-world behavior. \n\nYou have successfully bypassed the \"trick"
      }, {
        "text": "\" phase of differential equations and reached the core logic!"
